This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Additionally, for the specific case where $k=2$, we prove that a planar embedding is possible if and only if the graph is a complete bipartite graph $K_{p,q}$ with $p,q \leq 3$, unless one component consists solely of isolated vertices. Consequently, we provide a linear-time algorithm to determine minimum vertex splits required for planarity when limiting splits to two vertices. To support this algorithm, we introduce a new characterization of bipartite graphs with no crossings requiring more than nine edges to be planar, which serves as a crucial intermediate step. Ultimately, we present a concrete example of a bipartite graph where limiting vertex splits to two is insufficient to achieve planarity. The illustrations in this paper were generated using the "Bava" software, a new tool developed alongside this research to visualize and find optimal non-crossing drawings of bipartite graphs in a two-tiered format. This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere.
